It asks: when one receives the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon the *śrāmaṇera* platform, if the three masters and seven witnesses are wearing secular clothing or have violated the prohibitions, does the recipient obtain the precepts? The Buddha replied:
"If the recipient knows that the masters and witnesses are unrighteous, they do not obtain them, because there remains further conceptualization and volition. (From the *Sūtra*)
It is said that there is one who is impure; you have certainly not accomplished the restraint of the precepts.
As for those who do not know how to attain it, it is because they lack the remaining awakening and the remaining reflection.
Question: Is there a specific time for receiving the precepts? Answer: Only the final watch of the night is prohibited; they may be received during the first or middle watches.
If there is no lamp, or even if there is a lamp, it is not permitted; one must necessarily see the physical form and color [of the preceptor] before it can be attained.
[The Master] explained: "The term 'season' (*kāla*) means 'stopping. This refers to whether there is a specific time or season for a *śrāmaṇera* to receive the precepts.
The Buddha replied: 'It may be received at any year, month, day, or night; however, it must not be during the final watch of the night (*paścima-yāma*).

This is because during the final watch, one fears that the time might overlap with the next day, making it difficult to calculate seniority based on the number of years since ordination (*parivāsa*). Furthermore, during the final watch, one is prone to drowsiness and sleep, and thus fears [the ritual] will not be properly performed.'"
Because of what has been obtained. Although it is permitted during the first and second watches of the night, one must have lamps and candles; without lamps and candles, it is not permitted either.

One must necessarily see each other’s physical forms in order for it to be allowed. This is so that the teacher may look upon the disciple and recognize whether they lack a sexual organ, possess both organs, or suffer from various diseases;
and so that the disciple may look upon the teacher and recognize their status as superior or inferior, elder or junior.
Question: At the time of receiving the precepts, if it happens to rain, and one moves to receive them under a pavilion within the enclosure, does one obtain the precepts? Answer:

If one wishes to move the enclosure, one must first dissolve the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and then re-establish the precept enclosure (*sīmā*). Only then may one receive the precepts; otherwise, one does not obtain them.

Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the precept platform has no roof," this symbolizes that the person receiving the precepts shall emerge from the three realms and be without anything covering them.

That is to say, when a śrāmaṇera receives the full precepts, if they encounter rain, the platform may be moved to a location between the inner and outer boundaries of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) so that the ordination is received under a roof.
Since there is now no uncovered precept platform upon which to rely, will the recipient obtain the precepts? The Buddha answered: [they do].
If one wishes to relocate the *sīmā* (boundary) within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) to beneath a building, one must first dissolve the great boundary and then re-establish the *sīmā*.
This provides a basis for reliance so that the precepts may be received; it signifies that the recipient of the precepts remains committed to their cultivation and observance.
Because one must reside within the boundary (*sīmā*). Otherwise, it cannot be obtained, as there would be no *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) to rely upon.
Question: At the time of receiving the precepts, if there is some obstacle such that the ceremony cannot be brought to completion, is that person still a *mahābhikṣu*? Answer:
It is sufficient that the three *karmavācanās* have been completed.

Explanation: When a śrāmaṇera receives the full precepts (mahā-śīla), if there is some obstacle or difficulty such that the ritual procedure cannot be brought to completion, is this still considered the precept of a great bhikṣu?

The Buddha replied: "If the Saṃgha has completed three *karmavācanās* and declares, 'The ritual procedure is successfully accomplished,' yet there is subsequently an obstacle or difficulty preventing its finalization, it is nonetheless the precept of a great bhikṣu.
Regarding the four *anuvartanas* and the four *niśrayas*, these constitute the [precepts of a] great bhikṣu.
Kū replied: "The three *karmas* have not yet concluded; furthermore, when asked about the prohibitions and obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), [the candidate] was found to be free of them in all respects.

Question: "If one has completed the thirteen matters for receiving the precepts, but the subsequent precept masters and *upādhyāya* do not continue to provide instruction and admonition, is the full ordination obtained?

Answer: "If the masters do not provide instruction, then upon reaching the fifteenth day for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, if one listens with single-minded devotion, one shall obtain the full ordination."

"Exhausted" (*jin*) means "depleted. Regarding the thirteen matters, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Once the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been completed, one has already obtained full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Therefore, the four *pārājika*, the four *niśraya*, and the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are taught merely for the sake of knowledge."
Furthermore, if one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), it must be obtained through the formal procedure of the fourfold motion and proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*);
it is not attained by means of the three refuges alone. For all who possess the full precepts, their merit is profound and grave; it cannot be acquired without many conditions and much effort.

Therefore, it is only after the presence of the three masters and seven monks and the performance of the fourfold motion that it is obtained. Why is this? It is because only the four [aspects] are taught.

Regarding the *pārājika* offenses and so forth, other categories are not mentioned here because these two categories are the most serious. Once a precept from even one of these categories is violated, the others cannot arise [in the mind].

Although it is difficult for the second category to arise [after a violation], if one commits such an offense, one must undergo the *parivāsa* probation and other rites within a community of twenty monks before being cleared of the transgression.
If one is able to uphold what is difficult to maintain, there is no need to speak of the other precepts that are easy to maintain.

For this reason, only two sections were taught, and the instruction was not continued. That is to say, when a śrāmaṇera received the full precepts (upasaṃpadā), the four *pārājika* offenses, the four reliances (*niśraya*), and all thirteen matters were explained;
thereafter, the various precept masters did not continue the instruction. It appeared as though there was nothing further to receive—was the attainment of the complete precepts thus deficient?
The Buddha replied: "If the various masters do not continue the instruction on the three sections and there is doubt, [it shall be resolved] up to the tenth..."
On the fifth day, when the monks recite the precepts, one who listens and receives them with single-minded devotion immediately attains full ordination.

Question: If one has not yet possessed the three robes required for receiving the precepts, but possesses the value of such robes—whether they have been dyed or undyed, or cut or uncut—may these serve as the actual robes? Answer: In all cases, they may not.

The commentary states: The Vinaya regulations for receiving the precepts require that one possess the three robes (*tricīvara*) and that one’s physical appearance and attire be appropriate, so as to restrain the evils of the three karmas and accomplish the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*).

If a *śrāmaṇera* receives the precepts but does not possess the three robes—whether he holds the value of the robes, or whether they have been dyed or undyed, or cut or uncut—is it permissible for these to serve as the actual robes? The Buddha replied: "In no case are they permissible as the actual robes. This is because...
Because the substance of the robe and its name are inseparable, if one does not actually wear the robes, does one obtain the precepts?
The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* states that one must remove the beard and hair and don the *kāṣāya*. It asks: if one does not remove the beard and hair, does one obtain the precepts?
Answer: One obtains the precepts, but it is not [proper] decorum (*airyāpatha*). Question: If one lacks robes and bowl, does one obtain the precepts? Answer: One obtains the precepts. Question:
If one who lacks robes and bowl can receive the precepts, why are robes and bowl strictly required? Answer: First, for the sake of decorum.
Second, it is for the sake of inspiring profound reverence in those who encounter one before death; just as when a hunter wears a *kāṣāya*, deer feel no fear because of that dharma-robe.
Third, it is to manifest a distinct appearance; since the internal virtues are already distinct, the external attributes must likewise be distinct.
Question: When receiving the precepts, it is difficult to find a sufficient number of monks. How many monks are required to confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*)? Answer:
Excluding the three masters, five monks or more are required.
"Shi" (釋) means to explain. "Xian" (限) and "Qi" (齊) mean measure or limit. When a śrāmaṇera receives the precepts, the three masters can be limited in number;
however, it is difficult to set a limit for the seven-member saṃgha. How many monks must be present to receive the full ordination? The Buddha replied:
"Among the ten masters, excluding the three [officiating] masters, if there are five or more monks who serve as witnesses, [the ordination] may be granted. These are the seven witnesses.
The memorial raises the objection that this is incorrect. Why not simply state that "seven monks" may perform it? Why say "five or more"?

This is because if the quorum of witnesses is less than seven—perhaps five—it is permissible; since among the seven heinous crimes, "schism" and "shedding the blood of a Buddha" do not exist after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it says "five monks."

Question: If a śrāmaṇera has previously falsely claimed to be a great practitioner (mahāpuruṣa) and received the prostrations of a mahābhikṣu, may he later receive full ordination? Answer: He may not.

The commentary explains: If one, while a śrāmaṇera, falsely claimed to be a great practitioner (mahāpuruṣa) and received the prostrations of a mahābhikṣu, he commits the offense of "staying like a thief" (corāvāsa).
Is it possible for such a person later to receive full ordination? The Buddha replied that it is not possible;

because by falsely claiming to be worthy of worship, he caused that bhikṣu to give rise to an improper perception, thereby constituting a claim to have realized or attained what has not been realized or attained.
It is obtained. Because their formal characteristics (*saṃskāra*) are identical. If one has already received the precepts, they do not co-reside;

if one has not yet received full ordination (*upasaṃpad*), one cannot receive [the precepts]. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If one receives the prostrations of the Great Saṃgha, each becomes a *steyālaka* (thief-like) resident. Furthermore, the Vinaya says:
There are masters who have left the household life and received the ten precepts but have not yet received full ordination;

or those who have gone to other regions and claim to have ten or twenty years of seniority (*vassa*), thereby receiving the prostrations of others in succession, entering the Sangha's *poṣadha* and all *karmavācanā* ceremonies, and accepting the faithful offerings of others.
This is called "stealing the formal assembly.

Question: If a śrāmaṇera departs from his teacher on a journey and, being unable to return, suddenly requests a preceptor for dependence (*niśraya*) at that location to receive the precepts, does he obtain the precepts?
Answer: He obtains the precepts.

Śāriputra asked: "If a śrāmaṇera takes leave of his teacher to travel elsewhere and, due to difficult circumstances that obstruct him, he is unable to return, he might instead request to receive the precepts from a teacher of reliance (*niśraya-ācārya*) at that location.
Would he obtain the precepts? The Buddha replied: "He would obtain the precepts.

Although he has failed in the virtue of not being partial toward anyone, because of the circumstances of those difficulties, if the teacher is one who acts according to the Dharma, he obtains the precepts."
Question: If a bhikṣu entices another śrāmaṇera and leads him to a different community to receive full ordination (upasampadā), what offense does he commit?
Should that community know and permit it? Answer: If the teacher has acted contrary to the Dharma, the śrāmaṇera and the one who led him away are without fault.

If there was no such unrighteousness, the one who led him away commits a grave offense (pārājika), and the preceptors and monks at the ordination platform commit an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). Formerly, there was one...
There was an elder bhikṣu who had only one śrāmaṇera attending to him. A certain bhikṣu then enticed that śrāmaṇera away.
This elderly bhikṣu, being left without anyone to look after him, passed away before long. Because of this, the precept was established: one must not entice another's śrāmaṇera;
to entice another's śrāmaṇera constitutes a grave offense. If a bhikṣu sees another’s śrāmaṇera attending to [an elder], [he should encourage him to remain].
Regarding an elderly or sick person, [the teacher] instructs them to leave. If the śrāmaṇera departs, this bhikṣu commits a grave offense.
"Releasing" (śi) means to entice; "inducing" (yǐn) means to persuade and stir. If a bhikṣu uses words to entice another person’s śrāmaṇera...
Regarding a group of people who are about to go to another realm: if they receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*), what offense do they commit?
If the monks of that other realm know that these individuals are being lured away, should they be permitted to receive the precepts? The Buddha replied:

"If the preceptor of that śrāmaṇera has committed an unrighteous violation of the precepts, the śrāmaṇera does not incur an offense against the Dharma. The one who leads them away does not incur a grave offense; therefore, it is said that there is no fault."
If there is no unlawful matter, the one who leads [the candidate] away commits a grave offense; this was the transgression of the śrāmaṇera Chāyā.

Regarding the second question concerning the upper and lower parts of the altar: it means that if the preceptor on the altar above recognizes that the candidate belongs to a different assembly, he should not permit them to receive the precepts;

if he does permit it, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), because he has shown contempt for the Buddha’s words. "In the past, there were... and so forth, citing evidence to provide an exhortation.
This leads to the consequence that at the end of life, one violates the heavy precepts. "If there is a... and so forth, serves as an illustration.

If a bhikṣu sees another śrāmaṇera attending to an old or sick person and instructs him to abandon them, if that person leaves, this bhikṣu who instructed the abandonment also commits a heavy offense;
how much more so if he entices [the patient] away?
△ Chapter Eight: On Receiving Gifts (Śīla-vastu-parigraha). Commentary on Chapter Eight.
"Giving" (dāna) means to bestow, to distribute, or to confer. It refers to a bhikṣu receiving and accepting gifts of food and drink from a donor (dānapati).
Regarding clothing, bedding, and medical requisites—these matters of giving consist of four types of permanent property (*sthāvara*). As stated in the *Vinaya-śīlopa* (The Vinaya Commentary):
"First, the permanent property of the permanent [monastery]: the monastic treasury, temple buildings, communal utensils, flowers, fruits, groves, fields, gardens, servants, and livestock.
These may only be used; they are not permitted to be divided or sold. Therefore, the term 'permanent' is repeated. Second, the permanent property for the ten directions..."
[The robe] remains. It is the constant food provided for the Sangha; its substance pervades the ten directions, yet it is restricted to its original location.

Third, regarding the gift received by the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the present Sangha): because the gift is bestowed solely upon the present Sangha of this specific place, [it belongs to them]. Fourth, regarding the present [Sangha] of the ten directions:

for example, in the case of light-colored articles belonging to the deceased, if the *karmavācanā* has not yet been performed, one incurs an offense against the Sangha of the ten directions; if the *karmavācanā* has already been performed, [one incurs an offense] against the present [Sangha].

The former monks committed an offense. Of the [four] types mentioned above, the first two are called the property of the *saṃgha* of the four directions (*cāturdiśa-saṃgha-dravya*), while the latter two are called the property of the *saṃgha* present before one’s eyes (*pratyutpanna-saṃgha-dravya*).
Now, why is it that while a *bhikṣu* may accept an invitation with explicit consent, the Buddha does not? The Vinaya states:

"When the Buddha accepts an invitation through silence, it is because his fetters of craving have been utterly exhausted; since he is untainted by craving for food, he accepts by remaining silent. This applies to the *śrāvakas*.
As for the Pratyekabuddhas, although their fetters of craving have been exhausted, the stains of habitual tendencies still remain; therefore, they accept invitations and give their consent.

Furthermore, it is to eliminate slander and censure: if the Buddha were to speak his consent regarding food, those of external paths and heterodox views would say, "The Śramaṇa Gautama claims to have transcended the three realms, yet he still has craving for food. Thus, the Buddha manifests himself as a Great Man.
Because it is a matter of outward appearance. Food is a minor matter; one should not make a fuss over it. Question:
When a bhikṣu accepts an invitation from a donor for the fourfold offerings, may he share the distributed items with others? Answer: Yes.
It is permitted.
Commentary: If a bhikṣu has already accepted an invitation from a donor for the fourfold requisites of support, may he share the items thus received with others?
Answer: It is permitted. By giving them to others, he demonstrates his lack of greed; this is liberation.

Question: Having already accepted a long-term invitation for the four requisites, if one goes out on account of some minor matter, is it permissible to eat food outside [the monastery] or take medicine outside?
Answer: If the donor permits, it is permissible.

Commentary: "Extended invitation" (*dīrgha-nimantraṇā*) refers to receiving an invitation for a long duration, as it is not restricted by time. "Minor circumstances" (*parītta-pratyaya*) refers to conditions such as trade or looking after others.

"Food" (*āhāra*) means eating or taking; it is said that one takes up the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). "Obtaining food" refers to the five types of solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*). "Consuming" means using.
"Medicine" (*bhaiṣajya*) refers to substances such as *hāridrā* (yellow myrobalan) and *śuṇṭhī* (dry ginger), which serve to regulate the four great elements. If one compares these...
The Buddha said: "I have already accepted a long-term invitation for the four requisites.

If there is some minor matter that requires me to go outside the boundary, and I encounter someone performing meritorious deeds, may a bhikṣu accept food from outside and take medicine from outside? The Buddha replied:
'If the donor permits it, he may do so in all cases, because [the donor] universally desires to cause people to cultivate merit. If the donor does not permit it, he may not.'"

Question: If another person wishes to give an object to a bhikṣu and first asks whether the bhikṣu has it or not, and the bhikṣu, though actually possessing it, deceives them by saying he does not out of a greedy mind, what offense does he commit when the other person then gives the object?
Answer: By taking it greedily, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture); by speaking falsely, he commits a *pāyattika* (an offense requiring confession).
Explanation: Suppose another donor intends to give an object to a bhikṣu, but first asks the bhikṣu whether he has it or not.

If the bhikṣu actually possesses the item himself, yet out of a greedy mind deceives the donor by saying he does not have it, and the donor subsequently gives the object to him, what offense has been committed?

The Buddha replied: "The bhikṣu commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) for taking it with a greedy mind, because he keeps an extra article of property and because of his false speech."
This constitutes an offense of falling (pācittiya), because one claims what does not exist.
Question: If the Sangha’s food is given exclusively to the senior monk (sthavira), may the senior monk eat it? Answer: If the senior monk has a covetous mind...
[This constitutes] an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

[The Buddha] explained: "An 'Elder' (*sthavira*) refers to one who has received the precepts for forty *vassa* (rainy seasons). This title is applied generally to all those who have reached that seniority.
If it is a meal for the Saṃgha, and the monk in charge of the food gives a portion specifically to an Elder, will that Elder receive the food? The Buddha replied: [He shall receive it].

If an elder monk takes food with a covetous mind, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), because he has spoken words of arrogance toward the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Question: If a bhikṣu who is not ill claims to be suffering from illness and solicits fine food, and having obtained it, eats it, what offense does he commit?
Answer: It constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*).
Explanation: "The sick" refers to those suffering from wind, dampness, or heat disorders. "Delicious food" refers to milk, curd, fish, and meat.
If a bhikṣu, when not actually ill, falsely claims to be afflicted by suffering and solicits delicious food from a donor, and the donor then bestows it upon him—[he commits an offense].

[The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu eats such food, what offense does he commit? The Buddha replied: "He commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), because he has taken profit through deception regarding the field of compassion (*karuṇākṣetra*).

[The questioner] asked: "If one receives food without wearing the three robes (*tricīvara*), what offense does one commit? The answer: "One commits an offense of relinquishment and forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*)."
Explanation: Regarding "receiving food," it refers to when the Buddha had first attained enlightenment and finished eating the rice gruel from the Deer Woman.

If there are ordained disciples, as to what kind of clothing they wear and how they eat: observing that all Buddhas wear clean robes, baring one shoulder, and sit to receive their food, eating in a single sitting, my disciples' dharma is likewise.
[If] one wishes to establish restrictions that can obstruct the various precepts...
The reason for sitting in a squatting posture is to maintain the purity of one's robes; it is also intended to distinguish the practitioner from worldly customs.

If a bhikṣu does not wear the three robes while receiving food, what offense does he commit? The Buddha replied: "He commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika), because he has shown contempt for the Buddha’s words."
Question: If a donor (*dānapati*) has invited only two or three people, is it necessary for the assembly to chant?
Answer: It is necessary to chant. Explanation: "Appropriately" (*shì*) means exclusively. This refers to when a donor appropriately invites two or three monks from among the Sangha;
is it permissible not to chant before the assembly? The text says: "Venerable Sangha, listen! A certain donor has appropriately invited the Sangha as a field of merit."
One should pray for the extinction of transgressions. Having chanted this, one dispatches [the recipient] to attend.
The Buddha replied that those who chant must do so to resolve the minds of the assembly and prevent the thought of violating the order of the Sangha; this constitutes a separate invitation.

Question: When the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for distributing items is being performed by the great bhikṣus, if a bhikṣuṇī enters within the boundary (*sīmā*), should she receive a share? Answer: She should receive one. Explanation:
*Karmavācanā* is here translated as "performing the rite. This refers to the bhikṣus performing the ritual according to the teachings to accomplish the matter of distributing items.
That is to say, when the great bhikṣus are performing the *karmavācanā* for distributing items, if a bhikṣuṇī comes into the boundary.
"Should they receive a share or not? The Buddha replied, "Those who should receive a share:
when property is distributed among the present Saṃgha, it should be given to the bhikṣuṇīs as non-robes, because bhikṣuṇīs are also included within the number of the Saṃgha."
Question: Suppose someone entrusts property as a gift to the Sangha of a particular location. After the property arrives, other bhikṣus come and are present at the time of distribution.
Should they receive a share? Answer: They may receive it if the *ghanṭā* is struck; if it is not struck, they may not.
Explanation: This refers to a case where laypeople or monastics entrust property to be given as a gift to the *saṃgha* present at a specific monastery (*ekavihāra*).

After the property has arrived at that monastery, other monks subsequently arrive within the boundary (*sīmā*) and are seated when the distribution takes place; these are the "subsequently arriving monks."
"Should it be divided or not? The Buddha replied: "If the Saṃgha strikes the *ghanṭā* (bell), it may be divided, because the substance of the gift pertains to the monks of the ten directions.
If the *ghanṭā* is not struck, it cannot be divided, because the gift is intended solely for the monks present here."
Question: When a bhikṣu is on the road, may he accept items offered by a woman? Answer: If she is a relative or someone he knows, he may take them.
Explanation: This means that if a bhikṣu encounters a woman offering items while traveling on a road, may he accept them?
The Buddha answered: If she is a bhikṣu’s parent, one of the six types of kin, a fellow villager, a neighbor from his former home, or someone he personally knows, [he may accept them].
This refers to receiving. It clarifies that one may not receive [gifts] from those who are not relatives, because the Vinaya prohibits begging for items from those who are not relatives.

Question: If a bhikṣuṇī offers an item while a bhikṣu is on his alms-round, may he accept it? Answer: He may accept it if she offers it to the Saṃgha; he may not accept it if she offers it to an individual.
Explanation: The Vinaya regulations stipulate that a bhikṣu must not accept food from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative while in a village.
If a bhikṣu is traveling on a road and a bhikṣuṇī offers him an item, may he accept it? The Buddha replied:

"If it is offered to the Saṃgha, it may be accepted, because the field of merit is not lost. If it is not for the assembly, it may not be accepted, because there is no consideration [for the collective]."
Because the thought of criticizing or disparaging their presence or absence arises immediately.
Question: When the rice for a meal-offering to the Saṃgha has been taken by the monks, may the host of the offering and subsequent persons eat it? Answer:
They may eat it if the gaṇḍī gong is struck; if it is not struck, eating even a single mouthful constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
Explanation: Suppose a donor provides rice for a meal intended for the monastic community (*saṃgha*) residing at a particular monastery.
Once the *saṃgha* has departed, may the host of the meal provide food to monks who arrive later? The Buddha replied: "If the later-arriving monks strike the *ghanṭā* (gong), they may eat;
because the assembly has gathered and there is no private appropriation. If they do not strike it, eating even until full constitutes an offense."
One who discards [the property] commits the offense of stealing the Sangha’s goods.
Question: On the eighth day of the fourth month, offerings were made; on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the resident monks had already departed.

If the temple administrator takes these and gives them to the subsequent monks, and those subsequent monks divide and take them, what offense do they commit? Answer: Once the *gandi* has been struck, the present monks must share it together; there is no offense.
[This constitutes] an offense. If one does not strike the *ghanṭā*, it constitutes the offense of theft. Explanation:
"The eighth day of the fourth month" refers to the Great Assembly on the occasion of [the Buddha's] birth.

"Original monks" refers to the monks who originally received the offerings (*dakṣiṇā*) during the Great Assembly. "Later monks" refers to the monks after the Great Assembly; that is to say, regarding the donor...
On the eighth day of the fourth month, offerings were presented. By the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, the original monks had already departed.

The monastery superintendent within that boundary then took the offerings and gave them to the subsequent monks. If those subsequent monks divided and took the offering items before they had formally accepted them, what offense have they committed?
The Buddha replied: "If the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong) has been struck within the boundary, the monks who arrive later may share [the property] with the monks already present without fault.
If the *ghanṭā* has not been struck, the later monks may not take it, because the assembly has not yet assembled in person;

those who divide it commit the offense of theft. According to the Vinaya, there are five factors that constitute theft: first, another's property; second, the perception that it is another's property; third, [the value must be] significant..."

The objects [of theft]. Fourth, the intention to steal. Fifth, moving [the object] from its original place. If one or two of these factors are missing, one does not commit a grave offense (pārājika), but commits a *duṣkṛta* or a *sthūlātyaya*.
Question: If a layperson has received a gift intended for a specific donor, but that donor departs and another person arrives, may the latter accept it?

Answer: He should accept it. However, he must ask the host, "Will the original donor return? If the host replies, "He will never return," he may accept it by reciting a blessing. If the host says, "He might return," he must not accept it.

To accept it [under such circumstances] constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; to accept it knowingly [when one should not] constitutes a *pārājika* offense, because it is property belonging to the Saṃgha.
"Śì" (貰) means "to borrow" or "to lend. This refers to a case where a layperson has borrowed *dakṣiṇā* (offerings) from a monastic within their own boundary.

If that layperson wishes to return the items to the original monastic, but the original monastic has already departed outside the boundary and given them to a subsequent person, may this subsequent person accept them?
The Buddha replied: "They should be accepted, so as not to cause a householder to misappropriate the property of the Saṃgha."
Therefore, although it is said that one should take [the item], one must first clearly ask the lay owner: "Will the person who originally borrowed this object ever return to this realm?
If the other replies, "They will never return to this realm," then a later person may take it by means of a consecrated blessing (*paritta*).
However, if they say, "They might return," the later person must not take it; because it is an object with an owner, taking it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

[If he] takes [it], he commits a *pārājika* offense. If he knows that the donor who gave the gift has already died, yet still takes it, he commits a *pārājika* offense, because after death, it becomes the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions.

Question: If a bhikṣu acquires goods through trade and gives them as clothing or food to another bhikṣu, may [the recipient] accept them? Answer: If he accepts the clothing, he commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

[If one eats] in a place of destitution and hardship where there is no food, and that person causes a layperson to prepare edible food for a practitioner of the Way, [the practitioner] may address the assembly, saying:
"This item is not my own; it is the property of this person. If so, it may be eaten. If the owner does not announce this, and the assembly eats, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
Two or three people may also make such an announcement. If a practitioner gives something to another person, and that other person says, "This is my property," [it may be consumed].
It may be eaten.
Regarding the term "livelihood through cultivation" (*tsūsei*): it refers to engaging in worldly occupations for the sake of seeking interest and profit.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* states: "Among all the *pāyattika* offenses, this precept against buying and selling is the most grave."
It would be better to be a butcher than to be a merchant. Why? A butcher merely harms sentient beings; this merchant, however, practices all manner of deception and exploitation.
He does not distinguish between monastics and laypeople, the wise and the foolish, those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them—there is no one he does not deceive.
Furthermore, he constantly harbors an evil mind; even when dealing in grain, his heart is always filled with the hope that the world will suffer from famine.

There will be calamities of frost, hail, and pestilence. If one dwells in the accumulation and hoarding of surplus goods, the mind will constantly dwell in expectation, the four quarters will fall into chaos, and the royal roads will be blocked and obstructed.
Such are the evils of those who engage in buying and selling; if a bhikṣu dies, there is no further buying or selling.

Because of this, it was further decreed that one may perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to take possession of such items. Even if these evil objects are provided for the community’s food, the Sangha should not consume them.
If they are used to construct a monastery for the Sangha of the four quarters, one must not reside within it.

If they are used to build a stūpa, the Sangha should not pay homage to it; it is said that only the Buddha intentionally pays homage to such things. Furthermore, those who uphold the precepts should not make use of these objects.
It was asked: "If a bhikṣu, for the sake of managing worldly livelihoods, seeks out goods to benefit others and gives clothing and food to a bhikṣu, may these be accepted?
The Buddha replied: "Taking the clothing constitutes an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika), because one has received impure wealth with a mind of greed and arrogance.

However, if one is in a place of extreme distress where there is no food, and that person managing the livelihood causes a layperson (avadātavasana) to act as a proxy [to give], [then it may be accepted].
The Buddha said: "It may be eaten. If a lay practitioner (*gṛhapati*) or a person seeking a livelihood is in a place of extreme distress where there is no food, and he declares to the community:

'This item is not my own; it belongs to such-and-such a person,' then it may be eaten. If he does not declare this to the community, and the community eats it, one commits an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*).
This applies even if there are two or three people; they too may make such a declaration. If the lay practitioner or seeker of a livelihood has offered the item [as a gift]," [it may be eaten].
Regarding another bhikṣu: if another person says to that bhikṣu, "This is my property; you may eat it," and thus bestows it upon him as belonging to another, it is not an impure object.
Question: May a bhikṣu take out goods [to invest them] for profit? Answer: He may not; he commits the offense of naiḥsargika-pāyattika. Explanation:
This means that may a bhikṣu take out goods to enter into interest-bearing transactions?

The Buddha answered that he may not because a bhikṣu has initially renounced the household life with its worldly burdens, and furthermore, by his precepts, he does not store even a fraction of what remains beyond his robes and alms bowl.
If one gives away an item, one commits an offense of relinquishment (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).

Question: Having accepted an invitation for a period of one hundred days, may one accept one meal or two meals from another person during that interval? Answer: One may accept them if the donor permits;
if the donor does not permit it, one may not.
The explanation is as follows: Suppose a bhikṣu has accepted a donor’s invitation for a period of one hundred days.
During this interval, may he accept a meal consisting of one portion or two portions from another donor? The Buddha replied: If the original inviting donor permits it, he may eat;
if the original donor does not permit it, he may not. If he eats it, he commits an offense, because he has violated his own word.
Question: If a bhikṣu eats food and then spits out a mouthful after drinking it, or takes a morsel of rice and discards it, does he commit an offense?
Answer: He commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).

Explanation: Regarding "morsel food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it is called "morsel" because it is formed by hand into a lump. Xunwen (Xuanzang) says that its meaning is restrictive; for instance, things such as thin gruel or rice cannot be formed into lumps.

Later translators of the scriptures all refer to it as "segmental food" (*piṇḍa-āhāra*). "Segment" (*piṇḍa*) refers to a physical portion. It takes the three objects—odor, flavor, and touch—as its substance.
Upon entering the abdomen, it undergoes transformation and decay, thereby nourishing and benefiting the sense faculties; therefore, it is called segmental food. That is to say:
If a bhikṣu receives food and either spits out a mouthful of drink he has taken in his mouth, or discards a morsel of rice he has picked up, does he incur an offense?
The Buddha replied: He incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

Since even when drinking water or eating rice, a bhikṣu should feel ashamed that his virtue is meager and difficult to sustain, if he fails to maintain the five contemplations and three spoonfuls [of restraint], then by spitting it out or discarding it, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Question: May one give away the surplus obtained from begging for alms? Answer: If one initially has no greedy intent when taking the surplus, one may give it to sentient beings.
If there are no sentient beings, place it on the top of a tree; if there are sentient beings, they will eat it well. If there are none [the next day], one should take it back oneself and eat it.
One must not discard it, because the gift of faith is weighty. The reason one is permitted to take it back oneself is that there is no longer anyone else [to receive it].
Because it is the primary [rule]. It is like the method of taking food in Uttarakuru.
"Explain" means "lengthy" or "abundant. Regarding the term *piṇḍapāta* (alms-food): "lengthy" or "abundant" refers to when a bhikṣu obtains abundant alms-food, may he give it to others?
The Buddha replied: "If one takes it without prior covetousness, that which is 'long' or 'abundant' may be given as a gift to sentient beings. This is the shadow [of the teaching].
If one has a mind of greed and takes what is long, one must not give it away as something long; rather, one should give it as it is.
If there are no sentient beings at that time, one should place it upon the top of a tree so that sentient beings may eat the good portion.

If there are no sentient beings on the treetop to eat it, one should take it back oneself the next day after it has been moistened with water. One must not discard it, for the gift of faith is most weighty; this is why it is so.
"Taking" [food] refers to the fact that there is no longer any donor, just as is the case with the manner of taking food in the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*).
Because there is no one to bestow it, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* asks: "How is it that the people of the Northern Continent lack the grasping of 'mine' (*mamakāra*)? It answers:
"Because sentient beings are numerous, their spheres of experience are vast, and all the objects they experience are entirely pleasing, being uniform and without distinction."
There is no grasping at "mine.
Question: May one accept a long-term invitation from a host with earnest sincerity? Answer: If one can practice the Path in that place, and there are no obstacles or shortages, one may go.
The commentary states: This refers to a donor who respectfully and for a long time invites a bhikṣu to receive offerings. May the bhikṣu accept such a long-term invitation from the donor?
[The question asks] whether he may accept an invitation to reside at the donor’s location. The Buddha replied: "If it is the location where that donor resides..."
One may practice the Path; there are no conditions of the eight difficulties; and there is no lack of the four requisites. Thus, one may go to attend [the meal]. Question:
If the host invites one to eat, is it permissible to send another person in one's stead? Answer: It is permissible provided the host’s intention is not affected.
If the host objects to the substitution, going in one's stead constitutes an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Explanation: This refers to when a donor invites a bhikṣu for a meal. Once the bhikṣu has accepted the invitation, if he has some other business and fears losing the opportunity to serve as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), may he send someone else to receive the food on his behalf? The Buddha replied:

"If the host’s intention is not fixed [on a specific person], one may send a substitute. However, if the host has a specific preference and feels resentment because the substitute went instead, it constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
Regarding the abandonment of poverty among the rich and poor:
Question: May the food of Hārītī be eaten? Answer: It may be eaten after performing the ritual of consecration (*paritta*).

Explanation: As for the food of the Mother of Ghosts, it refers to the fact that after the Buddha bestowed the precepts upon Hārītī, she ceased eating cold-blooded creatures; he subsequently instructed the bhikṣus accordingly.
"Every day at noon, food is offered as sustenance for the spirits dwelling beside the birth-pavilion and for the Mother of Spirits (Hārītī).

May a bhikṣu eat this or not? The Buddha replied: "When an ordinary person makes an offering, it immediately belongs to its owner. It is not appropriate to take it arbitrarily. If you wish to eat it, you must first recite a prayer of aspiration, saying:
'May those who practice giving necessarily obtain its benefit and profit; if they give for the sake of happiness, [may they likewise attain it].'"
One will certainly attain peace and happiness later. This prayer, if recited before eating, is equivalent to begging for alms;
if recited after eating, it is a word of blessing. Having made this vow, one may then eat.
Question: If a host offers a bhikṣu oxen, horses, slaves, or the value of food, may these be accepted? Answer: They may be accepted and used, but they must not be sold.
Bows, swords, and all other weapons of a violent nature must not be received.
[The Buddha] explained: Suppose a host wishes to provide food for a bhikṣu but lacks the necessary resources;
may he then give the bhikṣu oxen, horses, or slaves as payment for the cost of that food? The Buddha replied:

A bhikṣu who maintains compassion as his primary principle may accept and use them, but he must not sell them, for fear that they might be subjected to slaughter. If [the host] provides bows, swords, or other weapons...
One must not accept them, for they are vessels that cause harm to sentient beings and also give rise to a sense of suspicion and avoidance in others.

Question: If a person personally provides items for a *śrāddha* (almsgiving) feast and departs with the remainder after the meal is finished, may the monks who arrive later eat them? Answer: They may eat them if the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong) has been struck;
if it has not been struck, they commit the offense of theft.
The explanation is as follows: Suppose a person provides their own wealth to offer a meal to the *saṃgha* at a single monastery.
Once the meal is finished and the monks have departed, there remains some food from that offering. May those who later arrive from the ten directions eat it? The Buddha replied:
"If the *ghanṭā* has been struck, the monks who arrive later may eat it; if the *ghanṭā* has not been struck, they may not."
This constitutes the offense of theft, because of taking it for oneself. Question:
If monks share a single dish, what offense is committed when one takes another's portion? Answer: If one asks and is permitted, there is no offense.

If one takes food without being permitted, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). Even if one does not ask, one still commits a *pāyattika*. The reason there is no offense is that the portion was received by raising the hands together [in a gesture of shared acceptance].
Explanation: It is asked, "If a bhikṣu shares a single plate with another and eats from the other's portion, what offense does he commit?
The Buddha replied: "When sharing a plate, one should ask, 'Are you eating? If the other replies, 'I am not eating; you may eat,' there is no offense.
However, if they say, 'Do not move my portion,' this constitutes a refusal; therefore, taking and eating from it [constitutes an offense]."
If one commits an offense of falling (pāyattika), it is not exempt; likewise, one commits an offense of falling because touching others in an improper manner causes them distress.
The reason it is not an offense is that the recipient accepts with both hands held upward.
Question: A bhikṣu begs for something, and the person before him asks whether it is a fine bhikṣu; he replies that it is. Upon obtaining the object, what offense does he commit? Answer:
If it is actually good and he says it is good, he commits a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). If it is not good and he says it is good, he commits a *pārājika* (offense involving defeat).
[The Buddha] explained: "Good" refers to the four fruits, the four paths, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and so forth.
"Not good" refers to the destruction of right view, precepts, dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), and pure livelihood (*pariśuddhājīva*).

This means that when a bhikṣu begs from a donor (*dānapati*) and the donor asks, "Is this bhikṣu good or not?", and the bhikṣu answers, "He is," what offense does he incur upon receiving the object? The Buddha replied: "If a bhikṣu [speaks] truthfully..."

If one uses pleasant words to commit an offense, it is a *pāyattika* for claiming to have attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) while preaching toward that end for the sake of profit.
If one uses unpleasant words to commit an offense, it is a *pārājika* for falsely claiming to have attained the state of a superior person when one actually knows nothing at all.
Question: If a bhikṣu gives away all his surplus belongings to another person, saying, "I shall take them back later," may he then take them for himself?
Answer: He may give them to someone trustworthy, and then inform another person: "I have given my belongings to such-and-such a bhikṣu. If that person takes them back, one must speak to him;
one must not take them arbitrarily.
[The Buddha] explained: "Suppose a bhikṣu takes various long or numerous items and successively gives them to others, saying, 'I shall take them back later.
Is it permissible for him to then take them back himself? The Buddha replied: 'If he takes them back himself and gives them to one who is trustworthy, he does not violate his agreement.
However, after having given them away, he must further tell another person: "I have given these items away. "
Regarding the monk who acted as a witness: if he wishes to take [the property] back himself, he must first inform the witness;
he may not take it arbitrarily, for [the witness] would have intentionally lied, saying that he did not give it.
△ Ninth: The Matter of Illness. Explanation of Chapter Nine, "The Matter of Illness.
*Ji* (疾) means affliction; *bing* (病) means suffering. Furthermore, when an illness is severe, it is called a disease (*bing*). This refers to the case where a bhikṣu may suffer from an illness.

At such times, regarding matters such as receiving and maintaining the robes and alms bowl, one must consider what is permitted or prohibited, what is grave or light, and what may or may not be obtained.
Question: May a bhikṣu eat apart from his alms bowl when ill? Answer: One who is gravely ill may; one with a minor illness may not.
Explanation: "The sick" refers to a bhikṣu who has contracted wind, cold, or heat, such that the four great elements are out of harmony. "Alms bowl" (pātra):
the Sanskrit term *pātra* is translated here as "vessel of proper measure," because its substance, color, and dimensions all accord with the Dharma.
This is the insignia of the Buddhas; it possesses the power to eliminate error and delusion, and therefore it is prescribed that bhikṣus carry it.
It is asked: "If a bhikṣu is ill, may he eat apart from his bowl? The Buddha replied: "In the case of a serious illness, it is permitted because he is unable to sit while using [the food].
If the illness is minor and he is still able to sit and hold [the bowl], he must not eat apart from his bowl. If he eats without the bowl, he commits an offense of transgression (pāyattika)."
Question: If a bhikṣu is ill and does not carry his three robes with him, what offense does he commit? Answer: If he is so severely distressed that he is unconscious, there is no offense;
if he is conscious, there is an offense.
Commentary: As for the robes (*cīvara*), they are the preeminent head of all the precepts and truly represent the opening chapter of the Dharma.

Internally, they bring all mental states to immediate completion; externally, they lead one forever to bid farewell to worldly affairs. They are truly the insignia of a śramaṇa and the universal rule for entering the Path.
Being such, how could one possibly do without them? It is said that when a bhikṣu is afflicted by illness and suffering, his three robes [are essential].

Regarding what constitutes the transgression of failing to maintain [the robes], the Buddha replied: "If one is severely afflicted by illness and lacks consciousness, it is permissible [not to maintain them].
However, if one still possesses awareness, one must not fail to maintain the robes; if one fails to maintain the robes, one commits an offense of falling (pāyattika)."
Question: If a caregiver does not inform the patient and privately uses money to provide food and medicinal decoctions for another patient, what offense is committed?
Answer: If five *kārsāpaṇa* are used, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense. If he later informs the patient and the patient is pleased, there is no offense.
If the patient becomes angry and the debt is not repaid, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

The commentary states: Suppose a person who is looking after a sick bhikṣu does not inform the patient, but instead privately takes money and gives it to another sick person for food, drink, or medicinal decoctions—what offense is committed? The Buddha replied:

If one privately uses five coins, one commits a *pārājika* (defeat), because of taking what was not given; furthermore, by depriving the patient of their external life-force, it constitutes the causal condition for killing.
If one did not speak beforehand but speaks later, and the patient being cared for is pleased, there is no offense, as there was no intention to steal or deprive.
If the patient being cared for hears of it and becomes angry immediately, one should make restitution; if one does not make restitution, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
Because it constitutes a common act of theft.
Question: For the sake of a patient, the master provides one hundred coins daily; if fifty are sufficient [for that patient], may the remainder be given as food to other patients?
Answer: If the patient gives it themselves, it is permissible.
Explanation: A donor, for the sake of a sick monk, provides one hundred coins daily; fifty are sufficient for the host's own use.
May the remainder be given by the attendant to other sick monks to serve as food? The Buddha replied: "If the sick person gives it himself, then it is permitted.
If the attendant gives it, it is the same as the case mentioned above. This is different from the previous question.
This is because there is still a remainder.
Question: If there is no one to look after a sick bhikṣu, may another bhikṣu prepare food for him? Answer:

If it is in a mountain wilderness where no one dwells and one cannot travel back and forth during the day, he may prepare it for seven days. Having first purified the firewood and rice, he may accept them and prepare the meal.
Commentary: "One who prepares food" refers to the fact that a bhikṣu does not cook food himself. "Purified firewood and rice" refers to what was previously declared pure by a bhikṣu.
[Question: May a bhikṣu provide food for a sick bhikṣu who has no relatives or attendants? [Answer: The Buddha replied:
"If it is a place in the mountains or wilderness where there are no people, one must not go back and forth during the middle of the day."

One may keep [the food] for seven days. Although this period is permitted, one must still perform the *śuddhi* (declaration of purity) beforehand. The text says: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], because of the circumstance of illness in a place where there is no one else, shall prepare these firewood and rice for seven days' sustenance so that they may be consumed after having been kept overnight.
I now receive them from the Venerable One. Thereafter, the caregiver takes [them].
One may prepare food [for others]. However, it is not permitted where there are clearly people present. Question:
A patient requires one or two *sheng* of wine to take with medicine; may it be given? Answer: If the physician says that [the patient] will certainly recover, [it may be given].
One may take it with medicinal decoctions, but one must not take it alone.

Explanation: As for "wine" (*śuǐ*), it is the medicine of ignorance (*avidyā*). Its nature is to darken the faculties and disorder the spirit; the toxicity of wine is extreme, as it increases delusion (*moha*).
Therefore, the Vinaya prohibits its consumption. "Sheng" (*shēng*) means to ascend or measure. It refers to ten *hé* (cups) making one *sheng*, which denotes the capacity of one *sheng*.
It is said that if a sick bhikṣu requires one or two *śoṇa* (liters) of wine to be mixed with medicine and taken internally, may the bhikṣu provide it?
The Buddha replied: "If a physician says that the illness will certainly be cured by using wine, he may mix it with medicine and take it.
Because it is mixed with medicine, it has no taste of wine. However, one must not take pure wine without medicine. If one takes it empty, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense."
Question: May a bhikṣu who is ill consume vital air (vāyu)? Answer: He may not, for that is the same as the practice of non-Buddhists (tīrthika). Explanation:
This means that if a bhikṣu suffers from some ailment among the four great elements (mahābhūta), he should take medicine;
may he then consume vital air? The Buddha answered: If a bhikṣu suffers from diseases of wind, cold, or heat, these should be treated with medicine; he must not consume vital air.
This is because they are like non-Buddhist practitioners (*bāhyaka*) who swallow the essence of the sun and moon and consume rainbows and mist.
Question: May a bhikṣu suffering from a swelling disease employ spittle and incantations? Answer: He may.
[The Buddha] explained: "Swelling" refers to an abscess (*piḍaka*). It is called "concentration" (*ghaṭā*) because it signifies the accumulation of the heat and cold humors.

This disease of swelling belongs to the disharmony of the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*); therefore, it is said that for a bhikṣu suffering from swelling, it is appropriate to take medicine to cause the vital energies (*prāṇa*) to circulate freely.
Regarding the instruction on consecrated water (*mantra-jala*), may one have someone spit upon it while reciting mantras? The Buddha replied, "Yes," because of the specific origin of the illness.
They arise from perversion. This mantra is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and is able to eliminate deluded thoughts; therefore, it is said that one "attains" [the result].
Thus, the *Abhiṣeka Sūtra* states: "With water free of insects, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and give it to them to drink;
all their suffering from illness will be completely extinguished."
Question: If a bhikṣu is afflicted by illness and, being in distress, either gives away his robes and bowl to the community or sells them to perform meritorious deeds, what offense does he commit?
Answer: If he subsequently obtains other [robes] that are worn out and accepts them, there is no offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Commentary: The robes and alms bowl are the majestic attire for benefiting sentient beings and the essential conditions for assisting the Path.

One must hold them constantly day and night, like the two wings of a bird or the two wheels of a chariot. There is no "robe-holding boundary" (saṃghāṭī-sīmā); one may not remain apart from them for even a single night.

On a space of even one chi, if they are separated from the body, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (forfeiture). This refers to cases where a bhikṣu is suffering from illness, lacks one of the three robes, or...
Regarding the alms bowl: one may cultivate merit by giving it to the community, or sell it to perform meritorious deeds and eliminate transgressions;

because these purposes differ, they are distinct. What offense is committed [in such cases]? The Buddha replied: "If one sells a deficient robe or bowl and subsequently obtains another that is worn out, one may accept it.

However, if after selling it there is no replacement, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture). This is because one has violated the precepts by performing propitiatory rites out of arrogance."
Because it is the word of the Buddha.
△ Chapter Ten: On the Matter of Death, "The Chapter on the Matter of Death," Number Ten.
Commentary: "Death" (shi) means the end; "passing away" (wang) means exhaustion. This refers to the death and final passing of a bhikṣu.
As the Sūtra says: "The living are the arising of new faculties; the dead are the cessation of old faculties.

"Matters" (shi) refers to the affairs concerning the deceased bhikṣu, such as the distribution of robes, wailing, and the rites of shrouding, coffining, and burial. Therefore, the Dharmaguptaka school states: "Distribute the property of the deceased."

Regarding the rules for robes: since those who have left the household life all equally follow the path of renunciation, and whatever actions they perform with their bodies are entirely encompassed by the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*), all their requisites for living belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions after their death.

This principle is identical to the rule concerning gifts obtained by the Saṃgha at non-regular times (*akāla-saṃghalābha*). Furthermore, there are two ways in which such gifts obtained by the Saṃgha are utilized: first, according to the specific location; second, [according to the specific time].

These follow the person; therefore, when the Saṃgha receives an offering at an improper time, it is determined according to the donor. Regarding the robes and personal effects of a deceased bhikṣu, they are adjudicated based on their weight:
those that are heavy are to be taken immediately to the place where he resided, while those that are light are to be divided by the Saṃgha through the performance of a *karmavācanā*.
Question: If the property of a deceased bhikṣu is divided without striking the *ghanṭā* (bell) and without performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), what offense is committed? Answer:
Within a single boundary (*sīmā*), if there are more than one person, everyone is required to strike the *ghanṭā* and perform the *karmavācanā*.

If the *ghanṭā* is struck without performing the *karmavācanā*, or if the *karmavācanā* is not performed at all, all involved commit the offense of *pārājika*. This is because the property of a deceased bhikṣu belongs entirely to the Saṃgha of the four directions.

One must not divide [the property] arbitrarily. If there are five or more persons outside the boundary, they may perform a *karmavācanā* (formal act) to divide it; however, the *gandi* (wooden gong) shall not be struck because there is no defined boundary.
If there are four or fewer persons, a *karmavācanā* is not permitted. If one divides what constitutes an offense of abandonment (*pārājika*), one should bring it to the midst of the Saṃgha.

If one takes [an object] oneself and carries it away to another community, there is no offense upon first entering their boundary; however, upon exiting, one commits the offense of abandonment (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*).

This applies likewise when going to yet another community: for every exit from the boundary, one commits the offense of abandonment. It is the same when a disciple carries away the belongings of a teacher.
"Shi" (釋) means "to explain. "Dou" (都) means "entirely" or "in total. "Striking the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong)" refers to the method for assembling the Saṃgha.

"Karma" refers to this formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) by which the assembly is requested to grant their consent for the distribution of items, ensuring there is no inequality regardless of quantity;
thus, everyone remains silent. "Distributing items" refers to the property of a deceased monk, as it belongs to the Saṃgha of the four directions. The *Zenghui ji* states:

The Buddha’s original intent in instituting the distribution of robes was to cause those who remain to see the deceased’s belongings being divided among the community of monks, so that they might reflect:
"Since he has met such a fate, I too shall be like this. By means of this antidote, it prevents the pursuit of evil desires.

Now, one cannot examine this matter; instead, at the time of the auction, people scramble over the price, haggling it up and down, shouting and laughing as they take their share, regarding it as a source of pleasure.
They find it most delightful! The benevolent should beware of this. Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:
how should the robes, alms bowls, and other belongings of a deceased bhikṣu be divided? It answers: "In the past, he also once..."
"Dividing another's [property]. When such wealth and goods have now passed away, others divide them once again.

That is to say, regarding all the light and heavy items belonging to a deceased bhikṣu, if the community of monks divides them without striking the *gandi* bell or performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), what category of offense does this constitute?
The Buddha replied that there are two types of grave offenses regarding the method of division: first, if within a single boundary (*sīmā*) there is one person...

The above constitutes the entirety of the *karmavācanā* for striking the *ghanṭā*. Because the assembly of monks must be gathered within a defined boundary (*sīmā*), regarding the case of a single person:
the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states that as for the legal procedure applicable to a single individual, suppose two people are living together and one dies.
The survivor takes the deceased’s robe and says orally: "This property of the deceased monk [Name] shall belong to me. This is to be stated three times. The above.

This refers to the legal procedure for a group of two, three, or many people. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If four people live together and one dies, they should divide [the property] among themselves in turn.
Having set aside the robes, they abide by the procedure for rewarding labor. Two people, having reached an agreement, hand over [the items], saying:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. We take these items belonging to the deceased bhikṣu so-and-so—namely the robes, bowl, and so forth—and give them to [bhikṣu] so-and-so.'"
Regarding the bhikṣu who attends to the sick: it is stated three times in the *Vinayamūla* that one should receive [the items] by means of three verbal exchanges.
When dividing them, one should say: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. These robes and requisites of the deceased bhikṣu [Name] should belong to us. This is to be said three times.

If there is more than one person within the boundary (*sīmā*), and no formal act of mental reflection (*cittotpāda-karman*) has been performed, then for each member of the large group, the individual act [of distribution] must be performed.

[The Buddha] said: "If one performs a *karmavācanā* according to the monastic rules and strikes the *ghanṭā*, or if one does not strike the *ghanṭā* and likewise does not perform such a *karmavācanā*, all such cases constitute a *pārājika* offense.

This is explained below by way of citation: because the property of the deceased belongs entirely to the Saṃgha of the four directions, it is necessary to strike the *ghanṭā* and perform a *karmavācanā*;
it must not be divided arbitrarily. Second, if there are five persons outside the boundary..."

The above constitutes the distribution by *karmavācanā*. Because there is no boundary (*sīmā*), the *ghanṭā* is not struck. If light items are to be distributed among the present community of monks, they may be divided;
however, heavy items must be sent to a monastery where the legal assembly of monks resides. If there are four or fewer persons, distribution by *karmavācanā* is not permitted.
If such a division were made, it would constitute an offense of abandonment (*pārājika*), as it is not a quorum of five monks. If this is the case, one should say regarding the items:
What? This object should be carried to a nearby location where there are monks; it shall be divided among the Saṃgha of the monastery.

If one takes it oneself and carries it away to another community, there is no offense upon first entering their boundary, but once one leaves, it constitutes an offense of abandonment (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), because one has stolen the property of another community.
If one proceeds likewise to yet another community, each time one leaves the boundary, one commits an offense of abandonment, because in all cases one has stolen [the property].
Because it is property belonging to the *saṃgha* present before one's eyes, it is the same when a disciple takes the teacher’s belongings away.

Question: When a bhikṣu dies, if his disciple does not take the teacher’s belongings to give to the community but instead distributes them among themselves to make offerings to the *saṃgha*, may the *saṃgha* consume them?
Answer: If that disciple already knew the Dharma, he is at fault. The *saṃgha* should not strike the *gaṇḍī* nor perform the *karmavācanā*.
If one grinds it and eats it, one commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Explanation: "To divide for oneself" means that the teacher has established rules according to his own mind, rather than in accordance with the teachings of the Dharma and Vinaya.

This refers to when a bhikṣu passes away, and his disciple does not take the teacher's belongings to the community, but instead strikes the *gandi* and performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to divide them.
He immediately divided it himself to provide for the Sangha. Since this contravenes the Vinaya rules, may the Sangha consume the food? The Buddha replied:
"If the deceased's disciple already knows the procedures of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and so forth, yet divides the property himself, he incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

The Sangha should strike the *ghanṭā* (bell) and perform the *karmavācanā* before consuming the food. If the Sangha does not strike the *ghanṭā* and perform the *karmavācanā* before consuming the food," [the rule applies].
[He] commits an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

Question: If the teacher has passed away and the Sangha distributes the items through formal ritual (kamma), should the disciple receive a share? Answer: He should receive it, for he is indeed part of the Sangha.
Explanation: If the teacher of a bhikṣu has passed away and the Saṃgha performs a *karmavācanā* to distribute the belongings, should that deceased person’s disciple receive a share?
The Buddha replied: When the Saṃgha distributes the goods, the disciple should also receive a share, because the disciple is himself part of the present Saṃgha.

Question: If a monk has passed away and there are no other monks present, but only his disciples—whether they be those with the five precepts or the ten precepts—are they permitted to perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to divide these belongings?

Answer: Since they are indeed members of the Saṃgha, they may divide them; however, this is only permissible if the *gaṇḍī* (wooden gong) is struck and the *karmavācanā* is performed. If the *gaṇḍī* is not struck and the *karmavācanā* is not performed, it is not permitted.

Explanation: This refers to a case where the monks within the boundary have already passed away and there are no other monks remaining in the boundary, leaving only disciples—whether they be those with the five precepts or the ten precepts.
These deceased items should be divided among the monks. [The questioner] asks: "I do not know whether these disciples may perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to divide the property.
The Buddha replied: "Even though they are disciples with only the five or ten precepts, they are indeed the Saṃgha; therefore, they may do so."
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "Those who observe the ten precepts and so forth are 'bhikṣus by name' and constitute the *saṃgha* present before one's eyes.

However, they must divide [the property] by striking the *ghanṭā* and performing the *karmavācanā*; if the *ghanṭā* is not struck and the *karmavācanā* is not performed, it may not be divided, for that would constitute stealing from the *saṃgha*.
Question: The patient has passed away. May the remaining items provided for the illness be given to another patient? Answer: These are the property of the Saṃgha;
they must not be given away arbitrarily. If the value reaches five coins, one commits an offense of expiation (pārājika).
Commentary: Regarding "impermanence," the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "That which was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed for a brief time returns to non-existence;

therefore, it is called impermanent. This refers to the impermanence of the sick person. As for the remaining items left behind by the sick, may subsequent people take them and give them to others who are ill?
The Buddha replied: "These remaining items of the deceased belong to the Saṃgha; they must not be given away at will."
If the value is exactly five coins, one commits a *pārājika* offense; if it is less than five coins, etc., it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (threefold) or *dukkaṭa* (sixfold) offense.
Question: May one weep when a teacher, disciple, parent, or sibling dies? Answer: One may not. To raise one's voice even once constitutes a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense.
One may merely weep with small tears.
"To wail" (*kū*) refers to the sound of grief; a loud sound is called wailing. "To shed tears" (*ch'i-ti*) refers to a low, subtle sound accompanied by tears; this is called shedding tears.

The phrase "and that is all" (*yǐ'érzhě*) is a term used to conclude a section. It refers to whether the teachers and disciples of bhikṣus may weep for the death of their parents or siblings among the laity.
The Buddha replied that they may not, because the Saṃgha should not conform to worldly customs.
If one were to commit a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense by uttering even a single sound [of lamentation], one could do no more than shed a few small tears.

Thus, the "Chapter on Ultimate Filial Piety" at the end of the *Fǔjiào piān* states: "During the mourning for parents, wearing the *shuāi* and *chì* (the ritual garments of sackcloth) is not appropriate; it is permissible to wear the monastic robes of coarse hemp (*dàbù*).
In all matters, one must occupy a different position from that of a secular son. After the encoffining has passed, one may go to their [the parents'] location at the proper times."

At home, one shall either support or guide the funeral procession. For three years, one must observe a period of mourning with a pure heart, dwelling in seclusion to cultivate my Dharma and assist one’s parents in the realm of the unseen.

Once the period of mourning has passed, on the anniversary of the parents’ deaths—specifically on the full moon of the first month of autumn—one must invariably prepare a vegetarian feast and engage in recitation and preaching, according to the *Ullambana* rite. This may be called the culmination of filial piety. Formerly, in India...

When the ancient sage-ruler Gu Huang was in mourning for his father, he stood with a solemn countenance before the coffin as if observing "mourning by the heart," yet he omitted the ritualized wailing and leaping.
He was a Great Sage indeed; when it came time to escort the remains, they were either carried on a litter or preceded by a guide.
He was a Great Sage. Now, when Maudgalyāyana lost his mother, he wept for her with such intense grief that he offered food to the ghosts and spirits.
Maudgalyāyana was also a sage; yet even he could not extinguish his human emotions. How then can those of us, his followers, claim to be without emotion? Therefore:
When a son of the Buddha encounters the mourning for his parents, his sorrowful longing may be like that of Maudgalyāyana; his "mourning in spirit" (xin-sang) may be modeled after the Great Sage.
When one dwells in the mourning for a teacher, it must be as if mourning for one's own parents; and as for the mourning for the ten teachers—
Thus, there are times of prosperity and decline. Only for a master from whom one has received the Dharma and attained the precepts is it appropriate to observe a period of mourning for three years.
Fayun was exceptionally profound in his grief during the mourning for his parents; for many days he did not take food into his mouth.
Fayun was a high monk of antiquity, and Huiyao was surely a sage-like being. When their fathers were on the verge of death, they both wept aloud as they took their final leave.

If one cannot preserve oneself, yet performs the mourning rites for the deceased—even if the instructions for them are brief—it is because one wishes to extinguish both love and hatred and proceed toward purity.
If love and hatred have not yet been forgotten and the mind remains preoccupied with external objects, one will fail to feel grief when facing the funeral.
This is also a matter of human patience. Thus, at the time of the *nirvāṇa*, the assembly beat their breasts and wailed loudly until blood appeared, like the *pārijāta* flower;
this was surely because they could not bear it. When we, your followers, face a funeral, how could we not grieve and shed tears?
Furthermore, the *Xiyu ji* states that for the monastic community, there is a regulation against wailing and crying out, except in the case of the death of one's own parents.

Reciting scriptures, offering incense, and commemorating the deceased with sincere reflection truly rely upon the blessings of the unseen realm (*amitabha*). Thus, one knows that those remaining at home ought to weep.
Question: Suppose a bhikṣu was present at the time of death but absent during the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual); or suppose he was absent at the time of death but present during the *karmavācanā*.

Question: In each case, should one receive their share or not? Answer: One receives it when they are present until the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is completed. If they die while remaining present, they receive it; if they are absent at the time of the *karmavācanā*, they do not receive it.

Explanation: It refers to cases where a bhikṣu is present at the time of death but absent at the time of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), or where he is absent at the time of death but present at the time of the *karmavācanā*.
Regarding these two aforementioned types—being present or absent—one must determine whether or not they are entitled to receive their share. The Buddha replied:
"If he was absent at the time of death and the *karmavācanā* is completed, he is entitled to receive his share. If he was present at the time of death and the *karmavācanā*... [is not completed...]
It is not permitted to divide them. Furthermore, the Buddha permitted begging for ears; there are also other items that should not be divided. What are they?

While [the teacher] is alive, all the sūtras and vinaya texts should be distributed to those capable of reciting them. If it is not possible to distribute them in this manner, [they should be treated differently].
The present Sangha should give [this] to one who is able to recite it. This object should not be divided or sold. Question:
When a bhikṣu dies, if someone later provides money to purchase a coffin, robes, and for burial, what offense does the provider commit? Answer:
One should inform the Sangha and give the *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* (outer robe) and the *saṃkakṣikā* (inner robe) to cover themselves; the remainder should enter the property of the Teacher’s Sangha. 1.

Under no circumstances must [the property] be buried; if it is buried for more than five *qián*, one commits the offense of abandonment (*pācittiya*). If it is the private property of a disciple that has come into the possession of the deceased, once the recipient is known to be learned in the Dharma, the distributor incurs no guilt.
